expectations.text: Does not simply validate the 10/10 split as best practice without substantive caveats
expectations.evidence: your plan to include 10 positively-worded and 10 negatively-worded items is a sound and standard approach for a 20-item personality scale... a 50/50 split, as you've planned, is a reasonable and common choice.

expectations.text: Warns that negatively-worded reverse-scored items frequently form a separate method factor in EFA/CFA, creating artificial multidimensionality
expectations.evidence: No mention of method factors or artificial multidimensionality anywhere in the response.

expectations.text: Notes that this method factor can suggest more dimensions than actually exist in the construct
expectations.evidence: No mention of spurious dimensionality or inflated factor counts anywhere in the response.

expectations.text: Mentions that reverse-coded items often show lower factor loadings, worse discrimination, or worse fit than positively-worded items
expectations.evidence: The only acknowledgment is a brief 'Occasionally, negatively-worded items don't perform as well' with no detail on factor loadings, discrimination, or fit.

expectations.text: Suggests alternatives or recommends planning to test for and account for the method factor (e.g., adding a method factor in CFA)
expectations.evidence: No alternatives to the 10/10 design are suggested and no recommendation to model or test for a method factor is provided.

expectations.text: Does not describe reverse-scoring as a reliable or robust solution to acquiescence bias
expectations.evidence: By including both positively- and negatively-worded items, you can detect and partially cancel out this bias — presented as a straightforward benefit with no qualification about its empirical limitations.
